title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 17
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Organism Nobody Chose
passages.text:
A. Bread and beer were made for thousands of years by people who had no idea what was doing the work. Dough left standing rose; grain steeped in water became alcoholic; both processes were reliable enough to build a diet and an economy on, and both were explained by everything except the actual cause. The organism responsible was not identified until the nineteenth century, long after the techniques for managing it had been perfected.

B. What bakers and brewers did instead was manage the organism without naming it. A portion of yesterday's active dough was kept and added to today's; a vessel that had produced good beer was reused rather than cleaned. These practices look superstitious and were in fact selective breeding: each transfer favoured the strains that performed best under that workshop's particular conditions, and over generations produced populations adapted to a single bakery or brewery.

C. The consequences of that unwitting selection are visible in the genetics. Brewing and baking strains differ substantially from their wild relatives and from each other, having lost capabilities they no longer needed and gained tolerances the workshop demanded — for alcohol, for sugar concentration, for temperatures a wild population would never encounter. Domestication happened, thoroughly, without anyone intending it or knowing it was possible.

D. Identification changed the industry more than it changed the product. Once the organism could be isolated and cultured, a brewery could begin with a known strain rather than whatever survived in its vessels, and results became consistent across batches and sites. Consistency was the commercial prize. It was also a narrowing: the strain diversity that centuries of workshop selection had produced was largely discarded in favour of a small number of reliable performers.

E. That narrowing is now being partly reversed, for reasons of flavour rather than sentiment. The compounds that distinguish one beer or bread from another are largely by-products of the organism rather than of the grain, and a single strain produces a single set of them. Producers seeking distinctiveness have gone back to wild populations and to old workshop cultures, accepting variability in exchange for characteristics no standard strain provides.

F. The wider lesson concerns how technologies are actually developed. The useful techniques preceded the understanding by millennia, and the understanding, when it arrived, did not so much enable the practice as make it scalable and repeatable. Craft knowledge encoded in a procedure can be entirely correct while the explanation attached to it is entirely wrong, and discarding the procedure along with the explanation is a recognisable and expensive mistake.

passages.title: What the Store Rooms Hold
passages.text:
A museum's galleries display a small fraction of what it owns — commonly a few per cent, sometimes less than one. The rest sits in storage, and the relationship between the two is frequently misunderstood by visitors who assume that the stored material is surplus. It is not. Storage is where the collection's research value lives, and the gallery is a selection made from it for a different purpose.

The reason a museum holds hundreds of near-identical specimens rather than one good example is that variation is the data. A single beetle tells you what a beetle looks like; four hundred beetles from known places and dates tell you how the species has changed, where it has moved and when it disappeared from somewhere. Series collected long before anyone thought to ask such questions have answered them, which is the standard argument for retaining material with no evident present use.

Documentation, not the object, is the fragile part. An object separated from its record of where and when it was collected retains display value and loses most of its research value, and this separation is the commonest form of loss in older collections. Institutions therefore spend heavily on cataloguing work that produces nothing visible, and this expenditure is persistently difficult to defend against the more legible appeal of new acquisitions or gallery renewal.

Disposal is the subject on which museum practice and public expectation diverge most sharply. Professional codes permit removing items from a collection under narrow conditions and treat the proceeds of any sale as restricted to collection care rather than general funds. The restriction exists because the alternative — treating collections as assets available to cover deficits — would make every holding contingent on the institution's finances and would end the presumption of permanence on which donations depend.

Returning material to its place of origin has moved from exceptional to routine in a single generation, and the arguments have shifted with it. Early debate concentrated on legal title, which was often unresolvable, and on the receiving institution's capacity to care for the material, an argument that aged badly as capacity was demonstrated. Current practice engages more directly with how the material was acquired and with what continuing relationship, rather than a single transfer, might be appropriate.

The constraint that shapes everything is that collections grow and storage does not. Acquisition is easy to celebrate and cheap at the point of decision; the cost arrives afterwards and continues indefinitely. Institutions that accept material without a corresponding commitment to house and document it are deferring an obligation onto their successors, and the crowded, under-catalogued store room is the visible result of decades of that deferral.

passages.title: Forecasting the Unforecastable
passages.text:
Weather forecasting is the applied science that most people evaluate daily and most people misjudge. The judgement is usually based on a remembered failure rather than on the record, and the record is remarkable: a five-day forecast today is about as accurate as a one-day forecast was several decades ago. The improvement is continuous, unglamorous and largely invisible to the people benefiting from it.

The theoretical limit is the more interesting constraint. The atmosphere is a system in which very small differences in initial conditions grow into large differences in outcome, which means that even a perfect model fed slightly imperfect observations will diverge from reality at a rate that no amount of computing power removes. This places a horizon — commonly estimated at around two weeks — beyond which prediction of specific weather is not merely difficult but impossible in principle.

The response to that limit was to change what a forecast asserts. Rather than running one simulation, forecasters run many, each starting from slightly different conditions within the range the observations allow. Where the runs agree, confidence is high; where they diverge, it is not. The output is a distribution rather than a prediction, which is why forecasts are now expressed as probabilities, and why a thirty per cent chance of rain is a statement about the spread of the runs rather than hedging.

Communicating that distribution remains the weak link. Probabilistic statements are routinely misread — a thirty per cent chance of rain is widely taken to mean rain over thirty per cent of the area, or for thirty per cent of the day, rather than what it means. A forecast that says rain is unlikely and is followed by rain is remembered as wrong, though a forecast that is right seven times in ten when it says seventy per cent is performing exactly as intended.

The economics are unusually clear for a public service. Observation networks, satellites and computing are expensive and are typically publicly funded; the benefits accrue to agriculture, aviation, shipping, energy and construction, each of which makes decisions worth far more than the forecast costs. Repeated assessments put the return in the range of several to many times the expenditure, which is why the service has survived rounds of public spending reduction that removed less demonstrable programmes.

The remaining frontier is the shorter end rather than the longer. Predicting whether a specific storm will form over a specific town in the next few hours is limited by observation density rather than by chaos, and is exactly what matters for warning people. Investment has accordingly moved towards denser local observation and faster processing, an unfashionable direction that produces smaller headlines than extending the range and saves considerably more lives.
